question: How can claims that a small subgraph implements an LLM capability be converted into statistical tests of mechanism preservation, localization, and minimality?

key_findings.claim: The paper separates the circuit hypothesis into preservation, localization, and minimality rather than treating one faithfulness score as decisive.
key_findings.evidence: A circuit is an edge subgraph made runnable by patching missing inputs. Mechanism preservation asks whether its task behavior matches the model, localization asks whether knocking it out removes task-relevant information, and minimality asks whether every retained edge matters relative to deliberately inflated circuits.

key_findings.claim: Three stringent tests operationalize an ideal circuit, while two reference-distribution tests quantify weaker sufficiency and partial necessity.
key_findings.evidence: The idealized suite uses a nonparametric equivalence comparison, HSIC permutation test for independence of the complement, and a Bonferroni-corrected edge test against random added paths. Flexible binomial tests compare candidate faithfulness or knockdown damage against random circuits whose size and source distribution determine stringency.

key_findings.claim: Hard-coded Tracr circuits satisfy the idealized criteria, but four literature-discovered circuits only partially do; induction is the strongest of the discovered set.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports all three desired outcomes for both synthetic circuits. Among discovered circuits, induction passes localization/independence and minimality, docstring passes minimality, and IOI/greater-than fail all strict tests. Nevertheless, flexible tests show all four are much less random than arbitrary subgraphs.

key_findings.claim: Circuit conclusions are materially dependent on the ablation intervention, task data, circuit-size definition, and null design, so p-values do not make the underlying causal construct objective.
key_findings.evidence: STR patching yields the paradox that removing the complete model can damage behavior less than removing a candidate circuit, whereas zero ablation removes this pattern. The authors also report that IOI can lose about 20 percent and greater-than about 50 percent of canonical edges with little faithfulness change, and acknowledge unstudied Type II error and setup non-robustness.

anchors.section: Partial necessity test and STR artifact

method.core_idea: Specify an explicit statistical population of comparison circuits for every mechanistic claim, then test candidate preservation, complement localization, and edge necessity instead of interpreting raw ablation scores without a reference.
method.mechanism: Transformer computation is represented as an attention-head/MLP edge graph. Removed edges receive zero or symmetric-token-replacement activations. Candidate task scores and L2 faithfulness are compared with random-walk circuits, complement circuits, or inflated candidate paths using binomial, permutation/HSIC, tail, and multiple-testing procedures.
assumptions: Attention-head/MLP residual edges are the appropriate granularity at which a task mechanism should localize.
The chosen patching value represents removal of information rather than an out-of-distribution intervention artifact.
Random-walk reference circuits and added paths constitute scientifically meaningful null populations.
The task dataset and score capture the behavior whose internal mechanism is claimed.

techniques.role: Tests whether candidate and full model have comparable per-example task performance within tolerance.
Tests whether circuit removal leaves model-correlated task information in the complement.
Uses edges from random added paths as a null for the effect of removing candidate edges.
Measures sufficiency and partial necessity relative to adjustable random-subgraph distributions.
Standardizes TransformerLens edge interventions and evaluation across benchmark circuits.

evaluations.setting: Two synthetic Tracr program circuits for proportion and sequence reversal.
evaluations.metric: Idealized equivalence, independence/localization, and minimality test decisions.
evaluations.result: Both ground-truth compiled circuits align with all three intended properties, serving as a positive control.
evaluations.baseline: The tests' random and inflated circuit reference distributions.

evaluations.setting: Induction and docstring circuits in small toy transformers plus IOI and greater-than circuits in GPT-2 small.
evaluations.metric: Strict test decisions and candidate faithfulness quantiles versus random circuits of varying size.
evaluations.result: Induction passes two strict properties, docstring one, IOI/greater-than none; all four outperform suitably sized random subgraphs in flexible tests.
evaluations.baseline: 100 random circuits for sufficiency/necessity and up to 10,000 sampled reference edges for minimality.

evaluations.setting: Iterative removal of edges ordered by minimality score and comparison of STR versus zero ablation.
evaluations.metric: L2 faithfulness and relative knockdown significance.
evaluations.result: Roughly 50 percent of greater-than and 20 percent of IOI edges can be removed without initial faithfulness loss; STR produces non-monotonic/paradoxical knockdown behavior absent under zero ablation.
evaluations.baseline: Canonical and empty circuits under the two patching schemes.

limitations: Author-stated: strict tests are difficult to pass, while flexible tests depend on circuit-size and reference-distribution choices.
Author-stated: Type II error for desired null-retention cases is not empirically characterized.
Author-stated: the benchmark circuits are not robust to changes in datasets, scores, and ablation setups.
Reviewer inference: the study tests six small/task-specific circuits and does not establish the circuit hypothesis for modern large-scale, distributed, or polysemantic capabilities.
failure_modes: A corrupted activation can create an off-manifold signal, so a large knockdown reflects intervention artifacts rather than causal necessity.
Random paths are not guaranteed irrelevant; inflated-circuit edges can interact destructively or redundantly with the candidate.
Bonferroni control becomes low-power for large circuits, causing unnecessary edges to survive the minimality audit.
Task-specific scores can miss alternative mechanisms or behavior changes outside the narrow evaluation distribution.
reusable_insights: Any circuit-quality number needs a declared null population; otherwise its magnitude has no calibrated meaning.
Triangulate sufficiency, necessity, and minimality because none alone identifies a mechanism.
Use synthetic compiled models as positive controls and random/inflated circuits as negative controls for mechanistic methods.
Repeat circuit claims across intervention values and dataset variants before treating localization as causal structure.
open_questions: How can null circuits be sampled invariantly across graph granularities and architectures without favoring the candidate topology?
Can equivalence and independence tests be designed with power guarantees appropriate for desired null retention?
What intervention distribution best approximates removal while staying on the model's activation manifold?
Do statistically validated circuits transfer across prompts, languages, model scales, fine-tuning, and related tasks?

competitive_landscape.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
competitive_landscape.difference: IOI introduced faithfulness, completeness, and minimality while reverse-engineering one natural task; the reviewed paper replaces circuit-space searches/raw scores with calibrated tests and audits IOI itself as a candidate.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: ACDC searches for sparse circuits and evaluates edge recovery against literature circuits; the reviewed work questions whether those literature circuits are valid ground truth and supplies post-discovery statistical tests.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
competitive_landscape.difference: This work systematically shows corruption and metric choices change localization results and recommends patching practices; the reviewed tests add statistical reference distributions but remain vulnerable to exactly those intervention choices.

competitive_landscape.title: RelP: Faithful and Efficient Circuit Discovery via Relevance Patching
competitive_landscape.difference: RelP replaces noisy local gradients with relevance propagation to approximate activation patching efficiently in larger models; it advances circuit discovery speed/faithfulness, whereas the reviewed framework evaluates a fixed candidate's scientific claims.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first suite of formal hypothesis tests that directly operationalizes the idealized circuit hypothesis and evaluates canonical circuits without exhaustive circuit search.
novelty_assessment.evidence: It specifies test variables, reference distributions, statistics, and error control; validates the suite on compiled circuits; and exposes redundancy and ablation artifacts in four published circuits.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Calibrating circuit claims against explicit nulls is an important methodological advance. Statistical rigor does not eliminate construct validity: reference sampling, graph granularity, patching, and task definition still determine what the tests mean.

reviewer_notes: Read all 29 extracted pages, including test derivations, algorithms, power discussion, all task/result appendices, ablation comparisons, and circuitry details. Primary arXiv records for IOI, ACDC, activation-patching best practices, and RelP were checked on 2026-08-23.
